title: Google's AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0: Mapping Gemini Usage in the Economy
pub: Google / Google DeepMind (AI & Economy ATLAS v1.0)
author: Zanna Iscenko · Scott Strand · Yiyuan Chen · Guillaume Aimard · Mihai Codreanu · Vivek Sampathkumar · Alex Imas · Julian Jacobs · Evalyne Muiruri · Juan Mateos-Garcia · Jia Jen Ng · Samirah Javed · Josh Martin · Omar Ajmeri · Denis Calin · Andrew Kim · Fabien Curto Millet · James Manyika

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The supplied ATLAS material consists only of bibliographic entries and provides no substantive claims, findings or recommendations from which to determine whether the source accepts, extends or rejects the cluster’s proposition about benchmark quality, governance and workplace meaning.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: The supplied ATLAS excerpt contains only bibliographic references and provides no substantive findings, arguments, methods or recommendations about realistic professional-task evaluation, reproducible scoring, automated judging or self-correction. Its position relative to the cluster proposition therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: ATLAS accepts the cluster’s distinction between technical exposure, actual use, automation and labour-market outcomes, then materially extends it with task-level Gemini usage measures classified by occupation, task type and user intent. It also advances a conditional distributional mechanism: augmentation may raise returns to non-routine skills and widen wage inequality, while treating employment effects as unsettled rather than inferred from exposure.
qs: As we show below, however, tasks being “affected” by LLMs is very different from those tasks being end-to-end automated.
Ultimately, this could lead to a deepening of wage inequality between this augmented cohort and those less able to use AI in their work.

st.t: Entry routes: Reduced hiring precedes broader displacement
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s qualified distinction between possible slower hiring of exposed young workers and no systematic unemployment increase, then materially extends the research agenda with task-level usage measures that distinguish automation from augmentation rather than treating occupational exposure as displacement.
qs: McCrory (2026) similarly find no systematic unemployment increase for workers with higher exposure but suggest these occupations are projected to have slower growth over the next decade based on BLS projections and that there may be evidence of slowed hiring of younger workers in exposed occupations.
We then distinguish tasks by user intent, asking whether AI is being used to automate or to augment human work, and by the expertise level those tasks require.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: ATLAS accepts the cluster’s core distinction between task-level augmentation and wholesale job replacement, and materially strengthens it with large-scale observational usage data showing broad occupational diffusion but shallow task coverage. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that usage and technical activity do not demonstrate realised productivity, labour substitution or legal outcomes, while adding evidence on unequal adoption and after-hours demand for legal assistance.
qs: This pattern is largely consistent with the labor-augmenting view that technology may help automate specific tasks rather than entire jobs.

First, because ATLAS measures de-identified interactions rather than productivity outcomes, we cannot yet answer how (and if) these micro-level task savings translate into macro-level total factor productivity increases.

st.t: Observed use: Capability predictions exceed workplace adoption
st.an: ATLAS adds task-level evidence from Gemini showing that observed workplace-related AI use is uneven across occupations and limited to interactions from three Google sources. This materially broadens the cluster beyond Claude while reinforcing that platform-specific usage patterns indicate current relevance, not job displacement or economy-wide adoption.
qs: The analysis in this section is based on AI interactions determined to be related to work tasks, aggregated across three Google sources (App, AI Mode, API).6 Throughout this section, we refer to these as “Gemini” interactions, to distinguish them from interaction with other AI products.

3.3    Occupational AI Usage  Starting with the US, looking at Gemini usage relative to population employment shares (Figure 1), “Computer and Mathematical”, “Business and Financial Operations”, and “Arts, Design, Entertainment, Sports, and Media” occupations are most over-represented in terms of AI use.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: ATLAS accepts the cluster’s core account of selective, assistive deployment and materially extends it with large-scale behavioral evidence: AI use is broad across occupations but concentrated in partial drafting, review, strategy and information tasks rather than end-to-end automation. It also reinforces the cluster’s warning that observed adoption cannot establish productivity, successful completion or future displacement.
qs: Instead, usage of Gemini for non-routine cognitive work is centered on Partial Drafting and Generation, Review and Refinement, Ideation and Strategy, and Information Retrieval and Learning.
Second, ATLAS v1.0 measures behavioral interactions, not definitive productivity outcomes.

st.t: Aggregate productivity: Task speedups shrink during scaling
st.an: ATLAS supports the cluster’s core distinction between task-level AI use and realised aggregate productivity. It finds broad but shallow, mainly collaborative usage, while stressing that interaction data do not measure productivity and that macroeconomic effects depend on firms and households converting capabilities into valuable tasks. Its household-value estimates are explicitly assumption-based rather than observed gains.
qs: First, because ATLAS measures de-identified interactions rather than productivity outcomes, we cannot yet answer how (and if) these micro-level task savings translate into macro-level total factor productivity increases.

It is largely an open question how high these numbers will be, depending on not just future capabilities, but also the ability of firms and households to translate them to valuable market and non-market tasks.

st.t: Annotation validity: Agreement cannot establish ground truth
st.an: ATLAS treats human agreement as validation evidence for economically meaningful classification, not definitive ground truth, and explicitly limits interpretation by metric sensitivity, taxonomy granularity, category guidance and dataset transfer. Its stronger claims about limited economic distortion are inferences from reasonableness and error patterns rather than demonstrations of real-world impact.
qs: The extent to which the exact values of kappa are interpretable and comparable has been questioned due to the sensitivity of the metric to the underlying distributions in the data (Sim and Wright, 2005; Warrens, 2010).

Overall, due to work/non-work sample coming from a non-ATLAS dataset, the applicability of the exact agreement values is less clear than for other variables in which raters had access to labeled ATLAS clusters.

st.t: Junior hiring: Stable unemployment can hide adjustment
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s distinction between broad AI exposure, actual usage and employment displacement. Its evidence shows diffusion across many occupations but limited task coverage and predominantly collaborative use, consistent with partial job transformation rather than demonstrated job loss. It does not directly establish stable unemployment or reduced junior hiring.
qs: AI has reached 68% of occupations globally yet it covers only a median of 21% of the constituent tasks within those occupations.
It is critical to acknowledge that AI usage is not synonymous with automation (the substitution of human effort with machines for specific tasks).

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: ATLAS supports the cluster’s conditional account: AI exposure and adoption do not establish automation, productivity gains or displacement, while effective augmentation may increase returns to non-routine human skills and advantage workers better able to use AI. Its wage-inequality claim is explicitly prospective rather than an observed effect.
qs: As we show below, however, tasks being “affected” by LLMs is very different from those tasks being end-to-end automated.
Ultimately, this could lead to a deepening of wage inequality between this augmented cohort and those less able to use AI in their work.

kp.k: ATLAS measures observed usage, not demonstrated economic outcomes
kp.d: The report analyzes 14,653,926 de-identified interactions from Gemini App, Google AI Mode and Gemini API between April 6 and April 19, 2026. Its automated pipeline maps conversation clusters to occupational, task and household-activity taxonomies. The authors distinguish this observational snapshot of adoption from AI capabilities, successful task completion, productivity gains and causal effects on employment or wages.
qs: Second, ATLAS v1.0 measures behavioral interactions, not definitive productivity outcomes.
A completed conversation does not guarantee that the user accomplished their intended goal, saved time, or produced measurable economic value.
The data captures the current frontier of AI adoption, rather than the technology’s potential impact and reach.

kp.k: Occupational coverage is broad, but task penetration remains shallow
kp.d: Above a threshold of 50 users globally per occupation, Gemini usage appears in 68% of detailed occupations, representing 88.4% of US civilian employment. This is occupational coverage, not the proportion of workers adopting AI. Task coverage requires at least 25 users globally per task: approximately 20% of tasks meet this threshold, while the median saturation among occupations with qualifying task usage is 21%. Only 3% of occupations have at least three-quarters of their tasks covered. The authors regard this pattern as possible support for complementarity rather than comprehensive replacement.
qs: Overall, we observe roughly 20% of tasks meeting this usage threshold in our sample.
For the group of occupations where at least one task has above the threshold number of user interactions, we observe a median task saturation of 21%.
Taken together, these results offer possible support for the notion that AI is currently serving primarily as a complement to existing work.

kp.k: Legal occupations show broad coverage despite modest interaction volume
kp.d: Legal occupations are among the office-work groups with comparatively broad coverage across detailed roles. The report explicitly distinguishes this breadth from volume: legal interactions remain modest relative to technology and finance. It also notes that the Legal group contains only seven detailed occupations, compared with 50 in Office and Administrative Support, qualifying comparisons between major groups.
qs: For instance, there are only 7 detailed Legal occupations while there are 50 Office and Administrative Support Occupations.
For example, Legal occupations exhibit broad coverage across detailed roles even though their overall interaction volume remains modest relative to tech or finance professions.

kp.k: Non-routine cognitive usage predominantly supports rather than automates work
kp.d: Non-routine cognitive analytic tasks constitute 35% of O*NET tasks but 65% of Gemini interactions. The preliminary intent classifier assigns less than 10% of conversations in this category to automation, versus more than a quarter for routine cognitive work. Other intents include partial drafting, review, ideation and information retrieval. These are classifications of what users ask AI to do, not evidence of completed automation; the automation category includes executing a core task or major sub-task end-to-end, and clusters may contain multiple intents.
qs: Non-routine cognitive analytic tasks comprise 35% of all O*NET tasks but 65% of Gemini interactions in our data.
Automation represents the intent of less than 10% of AI conversations in non-routine cognitive work appearing in our data.
In this subset, more than a quarter of AI conversations in our data are targeting task automation.
We cannot observe activity outside of Gemini so we cannot definitively say what portion of larger work, involving human effort, AI is being used to complete.

kp.k: Manual workers use AI for diagnosis and learning
kp.d: Although manual tasks are underrepresented, the report observes substantial assistance in physical occupations. Industrial machinery mechanics use AI to interpret test results and machine errors; over ten thousand sampled conversations concern automotive technicians and mechanics testing components, rewiring systems and inspecting wear. Automotive technicians’ multimodal conversation share exceeds twice the work average. Manual-task interactions concentrate on information retrieval and learning rather than physical execution or automation.
qs: This usage is often in tasks that are complementary to manual work.
For example, automotive service technicians and mechanics have multimodal conversation shares more than 2 times higher than the average in work AI interactions.
Manual tasks for which we observe Gemini usage are overwhelmingly concentrated on information retrieval and learning.

kp.k: Higher-paid occupations use AI more intensively
kp.d: US occupational usage intensity is measured as sampled conversations divided by occupational employment. A univariate regression associates 1% higher median earnings with 2.68% higher usage intensity; controlling jointly for education reduces the earnings coefficient to 1.86. The educational-attainment coefficient is 0.0076, implying 0.76% higher intensity per percentage-point increase in bachelor’s-degree-or-higher share. These occupation-level associations are not observed individual earnings gains. The authors suggest augmentation concentrated among advantaged workers could deepen inequality, but leave its realized distributional consequences unresolved.
qs: We find that workers in occupations with higher median earnings and education levels are more intensive users of Gemini.
The corresponding coefficients on univariate regressions are 2.68 (0.38) for log median earnings and 0.017 (0.003) for the bachelor’s plus share.
Ultimately, this could lead to a deepening of wage inequality between this augmented cohort and those less able to use AI in their work.

kp.k: Task expertise differs from workers’ earnings and qualifications
kp.d: Replicating Autor and Thompson’s method, the report estimates task expertise from the rarity and domain specificity of words in O*NET task statements, rather than directly observing workers’ competence. Relative to the taxonomy baseline, usage is particularly overrepresented in low-expertise cognitive tasks, especially non-routine ones, notwithstanding greater adoption in higher-paid occupations. The authors present improved model performance and progress in physical applications as possible reasons future usage could move toward higher-expertise or manual tasks.
qs: However, in our data, Gemini use is most over-represented relative to the O*NET taxonomy baseline task distribution, for the lowest expertise cognitive tasks, especially the non-routine variety.
More research is needed to determine the reasons for this pattern and its consequences for the labor market.
If model performance improves further, usage could increase for higher expertise tasks.

kp.k: Automating expert versus supporting tasks has different theoretical implications
kp.d: The authors report Autor and Thompson’s task-bundle model as a framework, not an ATLAS causal finding. In that model, automation of expert tasks erodes occupational entry barriers and depresses wages, while automation of inexpert supporting tasks increases the scarcity of remaining expertise, raising wages but reducing employment. Separately, the report cautions that even end-to-end task automation does not establish job automation because complementary work and organizational frictions remain.
qs: Automating more expert tasks erodes barriers to entry and depresses occupational wages, whereas automating inexpert tasks raises the scarcity of remaining human expertise, increasing wages but lowering employment.

We note that even in the case of observing higher rates of end-to-end automation in tasks, these do not necessarily equate job automation, as coordination costs, complementary tasks and organizational frictions are highly prevalent

kp.k: Unequal adoption could offset experimental skill equalization
kp.d: Drawing on Imas and Shukla and other cited studies, the authors contrast a catch-up scenario under broad, uniform adoption with a run-away scenario in which advantaged workers capture disproportionate gains. Proposed mechanisms include task selection, human judgment in checking and integrating outputs, and potentially seniority-biased hiring. These are literature-based mechanisms and conditional scenarios, not demonstrated ATLAS effects. The discussion emphasizes tool availability, business-specific innovations, formal training, management support and protected learning time as conditions for broader effective adoption.
qs: A key friction explaining this “micro-macro” gap is the endogenous adoption margin, i.e. the fact that in practice, adoption and effective usage of AI are not randomly assigned but self-selected by workers and organizations (Imas and Shukla, 2026).
Alternatively, if adoption remains endoge- nous and highly concentrated, the benefits of AI may accrue primarily to those who are already advantaged.

kp.k: Household use dominates conversational AI interactions
kp.d: For Gemini App and AI Mode, excluding API usage, 86.5% of interactions are non-work. The mapped categories cover 74% of ATUS categories and activities representing approximately 98% of Americans’ daily non-sleep time; this does not mean AI performs 98% of those activities. Global conversational shares include leisure at 26.4%, education at 20.7%, household activities at 11%, personal care at 9%, consumer purchases at 5.2% and professional/personal care services at 4.8%. The authors interpret correlations with human time allocation as evidence of a general-purpose household technology.
qs: Our data spans 74% of all classified statistical categories in the ATUS taxonomy, covering activities that represent about 98% of Americans’ average daily non-sleep time usage.
Non-work interactions account for 86.5% of all AI conversations, with nearly half concentrated in two domains: Socializing, Relaxing, & Leisure (26.4%) and Education (20.7%).

kp.k: Legal and bureaucratic assistance attracts disproportionate household demand
kp.d: Relative to US time-use shares, government services and civic obligations are represented almost twenty-fold, professional and personal care services more than seven-fold, and education about 5.8-fold. Legal services, alongside medical, financial and government services, attract substantial assistance, with nearly half of consultations across these domains occurring outside standard business hours. The authors suggest AI may reduce temporal and informational barriers to navigating institutions. They do not establish improved legal outcomes, reliable advice or reductions in unmet civil legal need.
qs: The biggest relative outlier is “Government Services & Civic Obligations”, which has almost a twenty-fold higher representation in AI usage than human activities.

These are cognitive or administrative tasks that represent significant transaction costs for households, such as Medical Care, Financial Services, Legal Services, Government Services, and Civic Obligations.
Notably, just below 50% of all conversations across these bureaucratic domains occur during evenings (M–F outside 9 AM–5 PM) and weekends.

kp.k: Household welfare estimates depend on assumed time savings
kp.d: The report’s household valuation is scenario-based, not a measured productivity result. Starting from 17.8 weekly hours of productive household activities and a $12.02 hourly replacement wage, assumed average savings of 0.5%–5% yield estimated annual US value of $14.9 billion–$149 billion; 2% produces just below $60 billion. The executive summary illustrates approximately $100 billion from average savings of 30 minutes weekly. These estimates omit leisure benefits and may miss quality improvements. Potentially greater benefits for women depend on adoption disparities as well as their larger household-work burden.
qs: Because there is no definitive historical or causal data on exactly how much time AI saves in the home, the analysis relies on a range of scenarios of time savings.
An average 0.5% time saving (approx. 5.4 minutes/week) yields $56 annually per person, scaling to $14.9 billion across the U.S. adult population.
An average 2% saving creates just below $60 billion in US economic value, while the more optimistic average 5% upper bound would create about $149 billion.

kp.k: Household substitution can obscure changes in measured productivity
kp.d: In her guest commentary, Diane Coyle argues that AI may change both market demand and unpaid household production. Faster or better household activity could substitute for purchased services, including tax preparation, while cost savings change consumption choices. Because conventional statistics principally measure market production, activity moving into households may appear as reduced productivity despite welfare gains. This is a conceptual argument about the production boundary, not an observed ATLAS displacement estimate.
qs: Innovations may seem to reduce productivity in economic statistics when they shift activity into the household because only the market sector is measured (Coyle, 2018).
For example, demand for market services such as therapy or tax preparation might decline and demand for other market goods and services increase.
Making sense of trends in the labour market and measured productivity requires taking account of both sides of the production boundary.

kp.k: Global adoption tracks wealth but varies across regions
kp.d: Penetration-adjusted conversational usage has an estimated GDP-per-capita elasticity of approximately 0.9. The lowest-usage country quintile represents approximately 17% of world population but 2% of usage, while the highest represents 11% and 30%, respectively. Some Latin American and Middle Eastern countries show high adoption. Internet-access adjustments reduce but do not close disparities. Lower-income countries have higher work-related shares despite lower overall per-capita usage; the authors offer goal-directed use, lower casual adoption and excluded enterprise subscriptions as alternative explanations rather than established causes.
qs: While the countries/regions in the lowest usage quintile in our sample account for roughly 17% of the world’s population, they generate just 2% of global usage.
However, this infrastructure adjustment alone does not fully close the global usage gap, indicating that other underlying drivers beyond basic access are also at play.
Alternatively, this pattern could be an artifact of a dataset limitation—specifically, the exclusion of Gemini Apps enterprise subscription data.

kp.k: Professional use does not strongly induce English switching
kp.d: The conversational dataset includes 143 privacy-cleared languages, with English accounting for just over one-third of volume. Non-primary-language usage averages 26% for work and just below 24% for non-work; English usage in non-primary-English countries is 14% and 13%, respectively. The authors interpret this as evidence against broad task sorting into English for economically important work. Non-primary-English interactions involve 9–12% more turns and 18–20% more tokens after activity and language controls, potentially reflecting interaction costs or greater within-category complexity.
qs: We find 143 distinct languages that occur in sufficient volume to pass our privacy-preserving thresholds.
For non-primary English language countries, the percentages of conversations in English are 14% for work conversations, and 13% for non-work.

These results suggest that utilizing AI in a non-primary language may be associated with a higher interaction “cost,” or that users systematically sort more complex queries (within a task category) into English.

kp.k: Classification uncertainty limits granular occupational and task conclusions
kp.d: Synthetic validation gives 93.7% accuracy for the balanced work/non-work classifier. Cluster-level exact matching is 71.57% for SOC major groups, 42.47% for occupation titles and 22.58% for specific O*NET tasks; ATUS major-category accuracy is 72.84%, falling to 23.70% at Tier 3. Human assessments of whether labels are economically reasonable are substantially higher, including 85.8% for task statements, but measure a different standard. The authors acknowledge synthetic-data biases, category ambiguity and the difficulty of inferring occupations from conversational content, favoring broader aggregations.
qs: Nonetheless, our work/non-work classifier achieves an accuracy of 93.7% on a balanced synthetic validation set that pools work and non-work observations.

Finally, although accuracy in matching the ground truth for exact O*NET task statements is 22.6%, the classifier assigns a task with the same Autor and Thompson (2025) task type as the ground truth for 70.4% of clusters.
On the other hand, however, the lower accuracy in assigning exact options at the most detailed taxonomy levels serves as a caution against over-relying on hyper-specific task analysis.

kp.k: Enterprise exclusions constrain conclusions about displacement and agentic work
kp.d: Taxonomized analysis excludes paid Gemini API content, including enterprise use through Google Cloud, alongside several other Google products. Paid API request counts enter geographic analysis, where IP geolocation reflects servers rather than necessarily end users and no API penetration adjustment is applied. Conversational geographic adjustments use web-referral proxies with acknowledged limitations. The report therefore cannot establish corporate integration patterns, emerging agentic impacts or whether AI is dampening entry-level hiring; its current augmentation findings do not rule out future displacement.
qs: First, taxonomized ATLAS v1.0 data does not currently contain paid usage of Gemini API, which includes enterprise usage via Google Cloud.
Second, because our dataset has yet to include enterprise-contracted logs, analysis of corporate-level integrations and the emerging impact of agentic workflows will come in the future.
Nonetheless, reassurance in the present should not preclude vigilance in the future, especially as the capabilities of AI models are improving fast (e.g. METR, 2026).

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The ATLAS authors describe broad but shallow, predominantly collaborative AI adoption, alongside disproportionately frequent household use for legal, financial and bureaucratic assistance.
pts.d: In this cross-domain report, Iscenko and co-authors report meaningful Gemini usage across 68% of detailed occupations globally, representing 88.4% of US civilian employment, but a median task saturation of only 21% among occupations with observed task usage. Legal occupations exhibit broad coverage across detailed roles despite modest interaction volume relative to technology and finance. Across work generally, non-routine cognitive tasks account for 65% of interactions but 35% of O*NET tasks; fewer than 10% of non-routine cognitive conversations are classified as seeking automation, compared with more than one-quarter of routine cognitive conversations. These are not legal-specific automation estimates. Outside work, the authors identify disproportionate use for legal help and other high-friction services, with nearly half of conversations across medical, legal, financial and government domains occurring outside standard business hours. They interpret this as potentially reducing temporal and administrative barriers. More broadly, they suggest AI could increase returns to human skill and widen wage inequality if effective adoption remains concentrated, while broad access and training could support equalization. They estimate potential household welfare gains under assumed time savings, rather than measuring realized gains. In her separately attributed guest comment, Diane Coyle predicts changes in household and market activity and suggests demand for services such as therapy or tax preparation might decline; she does not make an equivalent explicit prediction about legal-service demand.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is observational Google interaction data classified into economic taxonomies; welfare and future labor-market consequences are conditional interpretations, not measured outcomes.
pts.d: The report analyzes 14,653,926 de-identified interactions from Gemini App, Google AI Mode and the free Gemini API, summarized and clustered using an automated pipeline. Work clusters are mapped to SOC/O*NET occupations and tasks; non-work clusters are mapped to the American Time Use Survey. Occupational coverage requires at least 50 users globally, and task saturation requires at least 25 users. US employment, earnings and time-use statistics supply comparison baselines. Legal-service overrepresentation is based on conversation shares relative to reported household time allocation, not evidence of successful legal advice or replacement of retained counsel. Intent classification infers what users ask AI to do, not completed automation. Validation includes synthetic-data accuracy, human inter-rater agreement and human approval of label reasonableness; these are classification checks, not benchmarks of legal-output quality. Synthetic exact-match accuracy is 42.47% for occupation titles and 22.58% for specific O*NET tasks, while human reasonableness approval is 92.8% and 85.8%, respectively. Household valuations assume 0.5–5% savings in productive household time, valued at $12.02 per hour, producing approximately $14.9–149 billion annually across the US adult population. The authors draw on external experiments and economic models when discussing skill equalization, complementary judgment and possible seniority-biased demand; ATLAS itself does not establish those causal effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern a two-week April 2026 adoption snapshot; future automation, inequality and household gains depend on capabilities, access, organizational support and effective use.
pts.d: Published July 23, 2026, the report samples April 6–19, 2026. Its present-tense claims describe observed usage on included Google surfaces, not the full capability frontier or all AI adoption. Paid API content, enterprise-contracted usage and several integrated Google products are excluded from granular analysis, potentially underrepresenting professional deployment and agentic workflows. The authors say their snapshot does not support imminent massive white-collar automation and displacement, but caution that it cannot resolve whether AI is dampening entry-level hiring or will deepen the global digital divide. They explicitly distinguish task automation from whole-job replacement, noting complementary tasks, coordination costs and organizational frictions. Higher-expertise usage might increase as models improve. Distributional outcomes depend partly on broad tooling access, organizational innovation, training, management support and protected learning time. Household economic values require assumed time savings and exclude many possible quality improvements. No specific forecast date is given for these prospective effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source identifies legal professionals, household users of professional services, knowledge and manual workers, and differently situated populations as affected, without estimating law-firm restructuring or legal-market displacement.
pts.d: For legal professionals, the evidence concerns breadth of observed occupational usage rather than lawyer-specific productivity, employment, pricing or firm staffing changes. For the public, household legal and civic queries suggest demand for assistance navigating requirements, compliance and procedures, including outside office hours; the report does not establish closure of unmet civil legal need or improved legal outcomes. Higher-paid and more educated occupations use Gemini more intensively, potentially positioning already advantaged workers to capture greater benefits. Manual and technical workers use AI for diagnostics, troubleshooting and learning rather than physical task execution. Lower-income countries exhibit lower per-capita adoption overall, although some Latin American and Middle Eastern countries adopt at comparatively high rates. The authors find broad multilingual use rather than systematic switching to English for professional tasks, and suggest multilingual investment could improve access and interaction efficiency. Women could gain more from household time savings because they perform more household work, but adoption gaps could reduce or reverse that distributional effect. Coyle's proposed market-to-household substitution would affect households and providers of substitutable services, with therapy and tax preparation offered as examples rather than established displacement findings.
